articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $4.2 million tourism contract renewed without competitive bid
articles.dek: The deal with a Tallahassee marketing firm has rolled over three times since 2019. Commissioners say they're satisfied with the work. Records show no formal performance review.
brief: Escambia County has renewed its $4.2 million annual tourism marketing contract with Sachs Media for the third consecutive time without soliciting competitive bids
Public records requests reveal no formal performance metrics or independent audits have been conducted since the original 2019 agreement
Commissioner Jeff Bergosh defended the arrangement, saying 'if it ain't broke, don't fix it,' while two commissioners abstained from the July vote
articles.body:
The conference room on the third floor of the Escambia County governmental complex was nearly empty when commissioners voted 3-0-2 to extend a $4.2 million tourism marketing contract on July 18. The item appeared on the consent agenda. No one from the public spoke. The vote took less than thirty seconds.

That contract, held by Tallahassee-based Sachs Media since 2019, has now been renewed three times without the county seeking competitive proposals from other firms. The cumulative value exceeds $29 million.

County Administrator Wes Moreno told commissioners the renewal was standard practice.

"They've been a good partner," Moreno said. "We see the beaches full. The hotels are booked. What more do you want?"

What the county does not have, according to records obtained through a public records request, is any formal mechanism to evaluate whether Sachs Media's work justifies its cost—or whether another firm might deliver better results for less.

No metrics, no audits

The Flightline requested all performance reviews, audit reports and evaluation documents related to the Sachs Media contract dating back to its 2019 origination. The county responded with 847 pages of invoices, media placement reports and creative samples.

No performance review documents were provided. County communications director Kristen Michaels confirmed none exist.

"The contract doesn't require formal performance reviews," Michaels wrote in an email. "The Tourist Development Council reviews campaign reports at their regular meetings."

Those reports, also obtained through public records, consist primarily of Sachs Media presenting its own metrics to the council—reach figures, impressions, click-through rates. The council has no independent staff to verify the numbers or compare them to industry benchmarks.

The Tourist Development Council is an advisory body. It recommends how to spend bed tax revenue. Final approval rests with the county commission.

How the contract grew

Escambia County first hired Sachs Media through a competitive RFP process in 2019. The initial three-year contract was valued at $3.6 million annually.

When that contract expired in 2022, commissioners approved a one-year extension. Then another in 2023. Then another in 2024. Each extension included modest cost-of-living increases. The current annual rate is $4.2 million.

Florida law does not require competitive bidding for professional services contracts. Counties have broad discretion to negotiate directly with vendors they deem qualified.

But best practices published by the Florida Association of Counties recommend rebidding service contracts every five years to ensure competitive pricing and fresh approaches.

"You get comfortable with a vendor," said Erin Walsh, a public administration professor at Florida State University who studies local government contracting. "That's natural. But comfort can become complacency. Without competitive pressure, there's no incentive to innovate or control costs."

'If it ain't broke'

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, who voted for the renewal, dismissed concerns about the lack of competitive bidding.

"If it ain't broke, don't fix it," Bergosh said when reached by phone. "Our tourism numbers are strong. Occupancy rates are up. I'm not going to blow up a relationship that's working just to check a box."

Bergosh said he reviews Sachs Media's quarterly reports and finds them satisfactory. He acknowledged he has not compared the county's tourism marketing costs to peer counties or sought independent verification of the firm's reported metrics.

"I trust our staff," he said. "If they had concerns, they'd bring them to us."

Commissioners Steven Barry and Lumon May abstained from the July 18 vote. Neither responded to requests for comment.

What the money buys

The $4.2 million annual contract covers digital advertising, print campaigns, television spots, social media management and public relations for Visit Pensacola, the county's tourism brand.

Sachs Media's most recent quarterly report, presented to the Tourist Development Council in June, claimed the spring campaign generated 142 million impressions and drove 89,000 clicks to the Visit Pensacola website.

Those numbers are difficult to independently verify. The county does not employ analytics staff capable of auditing digital advertising claims. The Tourist Development Council accepted the report without questions.

Bed tax collections in Escambia County have increased 23% since 2019, according to county finance records. Sachs Media cites this growth as evidence of its effectiveness.

But tourism revenue has increased across the Gulf Coast during the same period. Okaloosa County, which uses a different marketing firm, saw 31% bed tax growth. Bay County saw 27%.

What happens next

The current extension runs through September 2027. Moreno said the county will evaluate options before the contract expires.

"We're always open to looking at the landscape," Moreno said. "But we're not going to change for the sake of change."

The county has no timeline for that evaluation. No RFP is currently planned.

Sachs Media did not respond to requests for comment.

The Flightline will continue to monitor this contract and the county's tourism marketing expenditures. Documents referenced in this report are available upon request.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: Downtown Pensacola's empty storefronts: A block-by-block count
articles.dek: Palafox and the surrounding streets have seen a wave of closures since spring. The Flightline walked every block to document what's vacant, what's coming, and what landlords are asking.
brief: The Flightline counted 34 vacant ground-floor storefronts in the downtown Pensacola commercial core, up from 19 at the same time last year
Asking rents range from $22 to $45 per square foot, with several landlords declining to list prices publicly
At least six closures since March cite lease renewals with rent increases of 30% or more
articles.body:
The paper signs in the windows tell the story before the numbers do. "Thanks for 7 great years." "Relocating to East Hill." "Space Available." One on South Palafox, handwritten in marker: "Couldn't make it work."

On a Wednesday afternoon in late July, The Flightline walked every block of downtown Pensacola's commercial core—Palafox Street from Main to Garden, plus the cross streets of Intendencia, Romana, Government and Zaragoza from Baylen to Jefferson. We counted every ground-floor storefront and noted which were occupied, which were vacant, and which showed signs of incoming tenants.

The count: 34 vacant storefronts out of 187 total ground-floor commercial spaces. That's an 18.2% vacancy rate, up from roughly 10% when we conducted the same survey in July 2025.

Where the vacancies cluster

The 100 block of South Palafox—the stretch between Garden and Main facing Plaza Ferdinand—remains fully occupied. So does most of the 200 block. The gaps start appearing around Romana and multiply as you move south.

The hardest-hit stretch sits on South Palafox between Intendencia and Government. Seven storefronts stand empty on that single block, including the former locations of a jewelry store, a women's clothing boutique, and a café that closed in April after five years.

The cross streets show similar patterns. East Intendencia from Palafox to Jefferson has four vacancies in a row. West Romana near Baylen has three.

What closed and why

The Flightline contacted owners or managers of 15 recently closed businesses. Six responded.

Four of the six cited rent increases at lease renewal as the primary factor. Jennifer Mullins, who operated a gift shop on South Palafox for four years, said her landlord proposed a new lease at $38 per square foot, up from $26. She declined and closed in May.

"I ran the numbers six different ways," Mullins said. "There's no version where I'm not losing money at that rate."

Another owner, who asked not to be named because they're negotiating with landlords for a new location, described a 40% rent increase proposed in March. They chose to close rather than sign.

The other two respondents cited different factors: one a partnership dispute, one declining foot traffic since a neighboring anchor tenant left.

What landlords are asking

Commercial listings reviewed by The Flightline show asking rents ranging from $22 to $45 per square foot annually for downtown ground-floor retail space. The median among 12 publicly listed spaces: $32 per square foot.

Several prominent vacancies carry no public listing. Phone calls to property management companies yielded responses ranging from "we're evaluating options" to "the owner prefers to negotiate directly with qualified tenants."

Marcus Chen, a commercial real estate broker with Pensacola-based Gulf Properties Group, said the unlisted spaces often signal owners waiting for higher-value tenants rather than filling vacancies quickly.

"Some landlords would rather sit empty for a year than lock in a five-year lease at rates they think are below market," Chen said. "Whether the market agrees with their assessment—that's the question."

What's coming

Not every empty storefront stays that way. Construction permits and interviews revealed at least five spaces with signed tenants preparing to open.

A Nashville-based hot chicken franchise has permits for buildout at 125 E. Intendencia, with a projected opening in late September. A local coffee roaster plans to open a second location on South Palafox in October, according to owner David Restrepo. A vintage clothing store, a yoga studio, and an ice cream shop round out the confirmed incoming tenants.

But the pipeline appears thinner than in previous years. Downtown Improvement Board records show 14 new retail openings in the first seven months of 2025. So far in 2026, the count stands at six.

The numbers in context

An 18% vacancy rate isn't a crisis by national standards. The average downtown retail vacancy rate across U.S. cities sat at 12.4% in the first quarter of 2026, according to commercial real estate firm Cushman & Wakefield. Cities of Pensacola's size ranged from 8% to 24%.

But downtown Pensacola marketed itself on a different premise. City officials and the Downtown Improvement Board have touted the district as a regional destination, a walkable core that bucks the strip-mall trends of the broader Gulf Coast. That pitch depends on a critical mass of active storefronts.

Councilwoman Ann Hill, whose District 6 includes downtown, said she's "monitoring the situation" but declined to characterize it as urgent.

"Some turnover is healthy," Hill said in an interview Thursday. "What concerns me is if we see these spaces stay empty for extended periods. That's when it becomes a problem."

What we didn't count

This survey counted ground-floor retail storefronts only. It excluded second-floor spaces, parking garages, and buildings under active construction. It also excluded the blocks south of Main Street and the Belmont-DeVilliers corridor, which operate under different market conditions.

A separate survey of those areas is planned for August.

The full block-by-block data, including addresses, square footage, and listed asking rents where available, is published in an accompanying spreadsheet at theflightline.com.

articles.label: Community
articles.headline: Blue Angels homecoming week brings 200,000 visitors. The people who live here have learned to adapt.
articles.dek: For residents near NAS Pensacola, the annual July airshow means closed roads, packed restaurants, and jet noise from dawn to dusk. Some leave town. Others rent their driveways for $50 a day.
brief: The Blue Angels homecoming airshow draws an estimated 200,000 visitors to Pensacola over three days, generating an economic impact exceeding $80 million
Residents within a two-mile radius of NAS Pensacola report practice flights beginning at 8 a.m. and lasting until 5 p.m. during the week leading up to the show
Some homeowners near the base have turned the disruption into income, charging $40-75 for driveway parking and renting spare rooms at triple normal rates
articles.body:
At 8:02 a.m. on Tuesday, Patricia Maldonado was standing in her kitchen on Bayou Boulevard when the first F/A-18 Super Hornet screamed overhead. The coffee in her mug rippled. Her dog, a 12-year-old beagle named Biscuit, crawled under the dining room table and stayed there until sunset.

"Seventeen years in this house," Maldonado said. "Biscuit still hasn't figured it out."

She has. By Wednesday she'll be in Mobile, staying with her sister until the show ends Sunday. She's done this for the past six years. She calls it her annual evacuation.

The Blue Angels homecoming airshow, held each July at Naval Air Station Pensacola, is the largest annual event in Northwest Florida. Visit Pensacola estimates this year's three-day show will draw more than 200,000 spectators and generate upward of $85 million in economic impact. Hotels from Perdido Key to Navarre have been booked solid since March. Restaurants along Palafox Street are hiring temporary staff. The Pensacola International Airport expects passenger volume 40 percent above normal.

For the tourism industry, homecoming week is Christmas in July. For the 15,000 or so residents who live within earshot of the base, it's something else entirely.

The choreography of disruption

The Blue Angels practice twice daily during homecoming week—morning sessions from roughly 8 a.m. to noon and afternoon sessions from 2 to 5 p.m. The team flies its full demonstration routine, which includes passes at speeds exceeding 700 mph and formations that bring six jets within 18 inches of each other.

The sound is difficult to describe to anyone who hasn't experienced it. At close range, the roar of a Super Hornet at full afterburner doesn't register as noise so much as pressure. It's a physical sensation. Car alarms trigger. Windows rattle in their frames. Conversations stop mid-sentence.

Dave Ehrlich has lived on Langley Avenue, about a mile from the base's western fence line, since 1998. He's a retired Navy commander who flew P-3 Orions out of NAS Jacksonville. He loves the Blue Angels. He watches every practice from a lawn chair in his backyard. He also hasn't scheduled a phone call between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. all week.

"You learn the rhythms," Ehrlich said. "You know when they're coming around for the high show, when they're doing the opposing solos. You plan around it."

His wife, Linda, takes a different approach. She drives to the Barnes & Noble on North Davis Highway and reads until the afternoon session ends.

The economics of inconvenience

On Cervantes Street, three blocks from the base's main gate, a hand-lettered sign reads: "PARKING $50 ALL DAY." The sign belongs to Marcus Webb, who bought his modest three-bedroom house in 2019. His driveway fits four cars. On show days, he makes $200 before noon.

"I took a vacation day Friday," Webb said. "I'll make more out here than I would at work."

He's part of a small but growing cohort of residents who have figured out how to monetize the chaos. On Airbnb and Vrbo, homes within walking distance of the base are listed at three and four times their normal rates. A two-bedroom bungalow on Barrancas Avenue that rents for $120 a night in June is asking $425 for Friday through Sunday. It's already booked.

Not everyone has that option. Renters can't list their landlord's property. Homeowners on cul-de-sacs with no street visibility can't sell parking. For them, homecoming week is pure cost—disrupted sleep, difficult commutes, restaurants with 90-minute waits.

"I love the Blue Angels as much as anyone," said Carla Dennison, who rents an apartment on Navy Boulevard. "But by Sunday I'm ready for them to go back to El Centro."

The infrastructure strain

Escambia County and the City of Pensacola begin preparing for homecoming months in advance. The coordination involves more than a dozen agencies: the Escambia County Sheriff's Office, Pensacola Police Department, Florida Highway Patrol, Escambia County EMS, the Naval Air Station security team and the Florida Department of Transportation.

On show days, Blue Angel Parkway—the main artery to the base—becomes one-way inbound from 7 a.m. to 10 a.m. Navy Boulevard and segments of Barrancas Avenue close entirely. Residents with addresses inside the closure zone receive placards allowing them to pass checkpoints, but most report adding 15 to 30 minutes to any trip.

"Friday afternoon, I needed to get to a doctor's appointment on Ninth Avenue," said Robert Kimball, who lives on a cul-de-sac off Navy Boulevard. "Normally that's a 10-minute drive. It took me 45 minutes because I had to loop all the way around through Warrington."

The show also tests Pensacola's hospitality infrastructure in ways that reveal its limits. Restaurant owners along Palafox describe homecoming weekend as both the best and worst days of the year—maximum revenue, maximum stress. Wait times at popular spots like Jackson's Steakhouse and The Fish House can exceed two hours. Several restaurants implement limited menus to keep kitchens moving.

Uber and Lyft drivers report surge pricing that pushes short rides to $40 or more. Some visitors, unprepared for the scale of the event, have posted complaints on travel forums about the difficulty of getting around.

The tradeoffs

None of this is new, of course. The Blue Angels have been based at NAS Pensacola since 1954. The homecoming show has been an annual tradition, with occasional interruptions, for decades. The rhythms of homecoming week are deeply familiar to anyone who has lived here long enough.

What has changed, residents say, is the scale. Attendance estimates have climbed steadily over the past decade. Social media has made the show more visible to audiences beyond the region. The transition from the legacy F/A-18 Hornet to the larger, louder Super Hornet in 2021 brought a new intensity to the experience.

"My parents brought me to the show in 1985," said Jennifer Odom, who grew up in the Myrtle Grove neighborhood and now lives on Scenic Highway. "It was big then. But it wasn't like this."

Still, most longtime residents describe the disruption with a shrug. They chose to live here. The base was here first. The Blue Angels are part of the city's identity in ways that transcend inconvenience.

Ehrlich, the retired Navy commander, put it simply: "You don't move to the beach and complain about the sand."

Maldonado, packing her car for the drive to Mobile, offered a slight amendment.

"You don't complain," she said. "But you're allowed to leave."

Biscuit was already in the backseat.
